author: frederick-brotherton-meyer
fields.title: The Secret of Guidance (For Teens)
fields.description: What subjects should I take? Which friends should I spend time with? What should I do with my life? F. B. Meyer, a London pastor whose books sold in the millions, wrote The Secret of Guidance for people asking questions like these. This teen edition retells it in plain words: how God guides, why your motives matter, how to use your head and pray, why you sometimes have to wait, what to do when the joy has gone, how to put facts before feelings, how to hand your worries to Jesus, and how to get through sorrow. Meyer’s own sentences are kept where they say it best.
fields.hook: How do you know what God wants you to do? A wise old guide to decisions, feelings, worry and hard times.

qa.question: Who was F. B. Meyer?
qa.answer: Frederick Brotherton Meyer was an English pastor, born in London in 1847. He pastored large churches in Leicester and London, spoke at conferences on five continents, set up homes for people in need, and wrote more than seventy books that sold in the millions. He died in 1929.

qa.question: How does God guide people, according to Meyer?
qa.answer: Through three things that agree: the Bible, the inner prompting of the Holy Spirit, and the way circumstances open up. He also says to check your motives, surrender your will, gather good information, use sanctified common sense, pray, and be willing to wait.

qa.question: What if I don’t feel close to God any more?
qa.answer: Meyer says feelings are not a reliable test of where you stand with God. Your standing in Jesus doesn’t change with your moods. Sometimes tiredness or stress takes away joy, as with Elijah, whom God gave food and sleep. If you feel low most days, please talk to a trusted adult or a doctor.

qa.question: Does God send bad things to punish me?
qa.answer: Meyer says firmly: don’t talk about punishment, because Jesus has taken the punishment for our sins. God can use hard times to grow us. But if someone is hurting you, that is never God’s will for you; please tell a trusted adult.

qa.question: What should I do with my worries?
qa.answer: Meyer says to hand them deliberately to Jesus, as you once handed him your sins, and to leave them with him. If worry or anxiety is overwhelming, talk to someone you trust as well.

qa.question: Is this the full text?
qa.answer: No. It is a retelling for teenagers in plain modern words, drawn from Meyer’s book and keeping his own sentences where they say it best. The full Secret of Guidance is also available.

fields.title: Willing to Be Made Willing
fields.body_html:
“For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.” — Philippians 2:13 (KJV)

Frederick Brotherton Meyer was born in London in 1847 and grew up in a Christian home. He felt called to be a minister when he was just sixteen, went to college, and became a pastor in Liverpool and then York.

In York he became friends with a little-known American evangelist called D. L. Moody, who taught him that a great preacher must also be a great worker. But the real turning point came later, in the city of Leicester.

There Meyer met a group of young people about to go to China as missionaries, among them a famous young cricketer called C. T. Studd. Their joy showed Meyer that something was missing in his own life. He realised there was one area, one “key” to his heart, that he hadn’t handed over to Jesus. He couldn’t bring himself to do it.

So he prayed an honest prayer: “I am not willing, but I am willing to be made willing.” And God answered. The surrender he couldn’t manage on his own was given to him.

From then on, Meyer’s preaching changed. Instead of just teaching facts about God, he helped people walk closely with God, filled with the Holy Spirit. His churches in Leicester and London grew to thousands of people. He spoke at conferences on five continents, set up homes for people in need, and wrote more than seventy books, which sold in the millions.

One of the best loved was The Secret of Guidance. It was written for ordinary Christians with real questions: How do I know what God wants? Why do I feel far from him? What do I do with my worries? How do I survive sorrow?

Those are questions many teenagers ask too. Which subjects should I take? Which friends are good for me? What should I do after school? What if I feel nothing when I pray?

Meyer’s first lesson is the one from his own life. If there is something you’re not willing to give to God, you don’t have to pretend. Be honest, and ask him to make you willing. That is a prayer God loves to answer.

One thing to do this week: think of one area of your life you find hard to hand over to God. This week, pray Meyer’s prayer about it every day: “Lord, I am not willing, but I am willing to be made willing.”

study_questions.question: What did the young missionaries in Leicester show Meyer?
study_questions.answer: Their joy showed him that he was missing something, because he had not given one area of his heart to Jesus.

study_questions.question: What prayer did Meyer pray?
study_questions.answer: “I am not willing, but I am willing to be made willing.”

study_questions.question: What questions was The Secret of Guidance written to answer?
study_questions.answer: How to know God’s will, why we feel far from him, what to do with worries, and how to survive sorrow.

fields.title: God Promises to Guide
fields.body_html:
“I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye.” — Psalm 32:8 (KJV)

Meyer begins by saying how much guidance matters: “so much of our power and peace consists in knowing where God would have us be, and in being just there.”

He reminds us how God guided his people in the Bible. Abraham left home with no map, only God. Israel followed a cloud by day and fire by night through the desert for forty years. When they were where God wanted them, food appeared each morning. Meyer says: “The manna only falls where the cloudy pillar broods.”

And the Bible is full of promises of guidance. “I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go.” “In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.” “The LORD shall guide thee continually.”

Meyer points out that God must guide us in small things as well as big ones, because big events often turn on tiny moments. A pebble can change the flow of a stream.

But maybe you feel that God guides other people and not you. You feel slow or confused. You can’t seem to hear him clearly, and you are so afraid of getting it wrong that you can’t work out what’s right.

Meyer has a beautiful answer. Think of a parent with two children. One is quick and catches on to every hint. The other is slower and struggles to understand. Does the parent only explain things to the clever one? No. The parent takes the slower child on their knee and explains it patiently, and loves them just as much.

So he says: “Oh! weary, perplexed and stupid children, believe in the great love of God, and cast yourselves upon it, sure that He will come down to your ignorance, and suit Himself to your needs.”

God doesn’t only guide the spiritual experts. He comes down to where you are. He knows how to speak in a way you can understand.

One thing to do this week: write Psalm 32:8 on a card and carry it with you this week. Whenever you face a decision, big or small, read it and say: “Lord, you promised to guide me. I’m trusting you.”

study_questions.question: What does Meyer mean by “The manna only falls where the cloudy pillar broods”?
study_questions.answer: God provides for us when we are where he wants us to be.

study_questions.question: Why does Meyer say God must guide us in small things as well as big ones?
study_questions.answer: Because big events often turn on tiny moments, as a pebble can change the flow of a stream.

study_questions.question: What picture does Meyer use to show God guides even people who feel slow?
study_questions.answer: A parent who takes a slower child on their knee and explains patiently, loving them as much as the quick one.

fields.title: Check Your Motives
fields.body_html:
“The light of the body is the eye: therefore when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light; but when thine eye is evil, thy body also is full of darkness.” — Luke 11:34 (KJV)

Meyer’s first practical step for finding God’s guidance is this: our motives must be pure.

Jesus said that when your eye is “single”, focused on one thing, your whole body is full of light. Meyer says that if you have been in the dark about what to do, the reason might be that your eye hasn’t been single. He calls it “a spiritual squint”.

What does that look like? Meyer explains that even when we are trying to follow God, self creeps in. We want to look good. We want people to praise us. We want what will make us more important. He says these hidden motives work “as the masses of iron on ocean steamers deflect the needle of the compass from the pole.”

Think of a compass on a ship. If there is a big lump of iron nearby, the needle won’t point north any more. It will point slightly wrong, and the ship will go off course without anyone noticing.

Our motives are like that. If part of you is choosing a subject because it’s what God wants, and part of you is choosing it because it will impress people, it becomes hard to tell which way is really north.

Meyer says: “So long as there is some thought of personal advantage, some idea of acquiring the praise and commendation of men, some aim at self-aggrandisement, it will be simply impossible to find out God’s purpose concerning us.”

That doesn’t mean you have to be perfect before God will guide you. It means being honest. Ask the Holy Spirit to show you your real motives, and ask him to give you a single eye, one main aim.

Meyer suggests the aim that Jesus had: to glorify God. Jesus said near the end of his life, “I have glorified thee on the earth.” Meyer says to make this the watchword of your life: “Glory to God in the highest.”

One thing to do this week: think about a decision you are facing. Write down all your reasons for each option, honestly, including the not-so-noble ones. Then pray: “Lord, give me a single eye. Help me want what brings you glory.”

study_questions.question: What does Meyer call mixed motives?
study_questions.answer: “A spiritual squint.”

study_questions.question: What picture does Meyer use for how selfish motives affect guidance?
study_questions.answer: Iron on a ship pulling a compass needle away from north.

study_questions.question: What single aim does Meyer suggest for our lives?
study_questions.answer: To glorify God, as Jesus did: “Glory to God in the highest.”

fields.title: A Yes in Your Will
fields.body_html:
“If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself.” — John 7:17 (KJV)

Meyer’s second step is that our will must be surrendered.

Jesus said, “If any man will do his will, he shall know.” In other words, if you’re willing to do whatever God says, you will be able to recognise what he’s saying. But if, deep down, you have already decided what you want, it is very hard to hear God.

Meyer says there is often “a secret controversy between our will and God’s”. We ask God to show us his will, but secretly we are hoping he will agree with ours.

Then Meyer makes an important distinction:

“There is all the difference between a will which is extinguished and one which is surrendered.”

God doesn’t want to crush your will, so that you become like a robot. He made you with a will, with desires, choices and personality. He only asks that your will says “Yes” to him. Meyer compares it to a willow twig, which bends easily in a skilled hand but is still alive and strong.

He describes watching a boy on a steamer as it came into port. The boy stood with his eye and ear fixed on the captain, ready to shout each order down to the engineers below. Meyer says he longed for his own will to pass on God’s will as quickly and accurately as that.

And then he gives the advice that came out of his own experience:

“If you cannot give, let Him take. If you are not willing, confess that you are willing to be made willing.”

This is really freeing. You don’t have to manufacture a perfect, surrendered heart before God will help you. Just tell him the truth: “I’m not there yet, but I want to be. Make me willing.” He will do it.

One thing to do this week: before you pray about a decision this week, pray this first: “Lord, I’m willing to do whatever you show me. And where I’m not willing, make me willing.” Then listen.

study_questions.question: What does Meyer mean by “a secret controversy between our will and God’s”?
study_questions.answer: Asking for God’s will while secretly hoping he will agree with what we have already decided.

study_questions.question: What is the difference between an extinguished will and a surrendered will?
study_questions.answer: An extinguished will is crushed; a surrendered will is alive but says yes to God, like a willow twig bending in a skilled hand.

study_questions.question: What should you do if you aren’t willing to give something to God?
study_questions.answer: Let him take it, and confess that you are willing to be made willing.

fields.title: Use Your Head, and Pray
fields.body_html:
“If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.” — James 1:5 (KJV)

Some people think that following God means switching off your brain and waiting for a sign. Meyer disagrees.

His third step is that we must gather information for our minds. He says God has given us “these wonderful faculties of brain-power, and He will not ignore them.” So we should find out the facts, learn from other people’s experience, and above all read the Bible.

He says the Bible is full of real people’s stories, so that “there is hardly a single crisis in our lives that may not be matched from those wondrous pages.” Whatever you are facing, someone in the Bible has faced something like it.

Then he says something very practical. God may occasionally ask us to act against our reason, but that is rare. Usually God guides us through what Meyer calls “sanctified common-sense”: thinking things through carefully with God, weighing the pros and cons.

He uses the story of Peter in prison. An angel woke Peter, unlocked his chains and led him out through the gates, because Peter couldn’t do that himself. But after a street or two, the angel left him to work out the rest for himself. Meyer says: “Thus God treats us still.” God does for us what we can’t do, and leaves us to use our minds for what we can.

His fourth step is prayer. “It is the law of our Father’s house that His children shall ask for what they want.” James promises that if we lack wisdom, we can ask God and he will give it generously.

Meyer suggests a particular kind of prayer for big decisions: ask God to shut the doors that are not his will. Put the whole matter into his hands from the start, and trust him to stop anything that isn’t right.

So for any decision: find out the facts, talk to wise people, read the Bible, think it through, and pray. That isn’t less spiritual than waiting for a sign. It’s how God usually works.

One thing to do this week: for one decision you are facing, make a list of facts you need, wise people you could ask, and any Bible passages that might help. Then pray James 1:5, and ask God to close any door that isn’t his will.

study_questions.question: Why does Meyer say we should gather information for our minds?
study_questions.answer: Because God gave us minds and uses them; he usually guides through careful thinking and sanctified common sense.

study_questions.question: What does the story of Peter and the angel teach about guidance?
study_questions.answer: God does for us what we cannot do, then leaves us to use our own minds for what we can.

study_questions.question: What kind of prayer does Meyer suggest for big decisions?
study_questions.answer: Asking God to shut the doors that are not his will.

fields.title: The Next Step
fields.body_html:
“The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD: and he delighteth in his way.” — Psalm 37:23 (KJV)

Meyer’s fifth step is the hardest for many of us: wait for God’s plan to unfold.

He says God guides through three things: impressions inside us from the Holy Spirit, his Word in the Bible, and providence, meaning how circumstances work out around us. We should wait until all three point the same way.

Waiting is hard, especially when everyone is telling you to decide now. Meyer reminds us of Israel at the Red Sea, with the Egyptian army behind them, cliffs on either side and the sea in front. It looked as if they had to do something. But God told them to stand still and see his salvation.

He also mentions King Saul, who got tired of waiting for the prophet Samuel and offered a sacrifice himself. Meyer calls it “the great mistake of his life.”

Meyer’s simple rule is this:

“If you do not know what you ought to do, stand still until you do.”

And when the time comes, he says, the circumstances will begin to line up, like lights multiplying as a train at night gets closer to a town. You will become sure.

Then Meyer says something very reassuring. We often think God isn’t guiding us because we can’t see far ahead. But that isn’t how God works. He promises to order our steps, not to show us the whole map.

“Not the next mile, but the next yard. Not the whole pattern, but the next stitch in the canvas.”

You might not know what you’ll do after school, or where you’ll be in ten years. That’s OK. God hasn’t promised to show you that yet. He has promised to guide your next step. Take it, and trust him for the one after.

Meyer ends this chapter with his own testimony: “after months of waiting and prayer, I have become absolutely sure of the Guidance of my heavenly Father.”

One thing to do this week: if you are anxious about the future, write down just the next step you know to take, this week or today. Do that step, and pray: “Lord, I trust you for the step after this one.”

study_questions.question: What three things does Meyer say should agree when God guides?
study_questions.answer: The inner prompting of the Spirit, the Word of God, and the circumstances of providence.

study_questions.question: What is Meyer’s rule when you don’t know what to do?
study_questions.answer: Stand still until you do.

study_questions.question: How much of the way does God usually show us?
study_questions.answer: Not the next mile but the next yard; not the whole pattern but the next stitch.

fields.title: When the Joy Has Gone
fields.body_html:
“And as he lay and slept under a juniper tree, behold, then an angel touched him, and said unto him, Arise and eat.” — 1 Kings 19:5 (KJV)

Meyer wrote a chapter called “Where Am I Wrong?” for Christians who see joy in others but feel none themselves.

First he says something important: not everyone feels things the same way. Some people naturally tend towards feeling low. That doesn’t make them worse Christians. And he says that our feelings are not a reliable test of our spiritual state:

“In other words, absence of joy does not always prove that the heart is wrong.”

Sometimes, he says, we are just exhausted, like the prophet Elijah. After a huge spiritual victory and then running for his life, Elijah lay down in the desert and asked to die. And God didn’t tell him off. Meyer notes that God met him “not with rebuke, but with food and sleep.”

That is worth remembering. Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is eat a proper meal and get some sleep.

Meyer does go on to say that when people feel low they should simply carry it quietly. Today we know more. If you feel down most days, or flat and empty for weeks, or have thoughts of not wanting to live, that is not something to carry alone or in silence. Please talk to a trusted adult, a school counsellor or a doctor. Depression is real, it is nobody’s fault, and help really does work.

Meyer’s most helpful point is the difference between your standing and your experience. Your experience, how you feel, changes like the weather. But your standing in Jesus, the fact that you belong to him, doesn’t change at all.

He uses a money picture. Your standing in Jesus is like “invested capital”. Your emotions are like “spending money”, always going in and out of your pocket. Your capital doesn’t shrink just because your pocket money is low this week.

So he says: “Cease to consider how you feel, and build on the immovable rock of what Jesus is, and has done.” And he adds: “God does not hold us responsible for what we feel, but for what we will.” You can’t always choose your feelings. You can choose to keep trusting.

One thing to do this week: if you feel spiritually flat this week, look after your body: eat well, sleep properly, get outside. Then remind yourself every day: “My standing in Jesus hasn’t changed.” If the low feeling goes on, tell someone you trust.

study_questions.question: Does a lack of joy always mean something is wrong with your heart?
study_questions.answer: No; Meyer says absence of joy does not always prove the heart is wrong.

study_questions.question: How did God treat Elijah when he was exhausted and wanted to die?
study_questions.answer: Not with rebuke, but with food and sleep.

study_questions.answer: Our experience, how we feel, changes constantly; our standing in Jesus never changes.

fields.title: Fact, Faith, Feeling
fields.body_html:
“But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name.” — John 1:12 (KJV)

Meyer has a chapter with a catchy title: Fact! Faith! Feeling! He says these three words have to come in the right order.

Most people try to put feeling first. They wait to feel close to God before they believe anything. Meyer says that is like trying to build the top floor of a house before laying the foundations.

The right order is: God’s facts first, as the foundation. Then our faith, resting on those facts. Then feelings, which come, he says, “it may be at once, or after the lapse of days and months, as God will.”

He compares God’s facts to stepping stones across a stream. From a distance you wonder whether you can get across. But when you come down to the water and see how firmly the stones are set, you can trust them and step from one to the next.

So what are the facts? Meyer lists some. It is a fact that God loves you with “the tenderest and most particular love”. You may not feel it, he says, just as the sun can be shining on a house with all its curtains shut, but your not feeling it doesn’t change it.

It is a fact that because of Jesus, nothing stands in the way of your being forgiven and accepted. And it is a fact that as soon as you trust Christ, you are God’s child. “You may be a prodigal or inconsistent child,” Meyer says, “but you are a child.”

He tells a story from the end of the American Civil War. After peace was signed, some soldiers kept hiding in the woods, starving, because they didn’t know or didn’t believe the war was over. Their families were waiting for them at home. Their not believing didn’t change the fact that peace had been declared. It just kept them miserable.

That is what happens when we let feelings rule. The facts are true whether we feel them or not. Stand on the facts, trust them, and in God’s time the feelings will usually follow.

One thing to do this week: write down three facts from the Bible about God’s love and your place in his family, for example John 1:12, Romans 5:8 and Romans 8:1. This week, read them every morning before you check how you feel.

study_questions.question: What is the right order of fact, faith and feeling?
study_questions.answer: God’s facts first, then our faith resting on them, then feelings as God gives them.

study_questions.question: What picture does Meyer use for God’s facts?
study_questions.answer: Stepping stones firmly set across a stream.

study_questions.question: What does the story of the soldiers hiding in the woods teach?
study_questions.answer: Not believing the good news doesn’t change it; it only keeps us miserable.

fields.title: Put Them in Christ’s Bag
fields.body_html:
“Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.” — 1 Peter 5:7 (KJV)

Meyer has a whole chapter about burdens, the worries and anxieties we carry around.

He describes something many of us know. Before we are properly awake in the morning, a voice starts listing everything that will go wrong today: the test, the awkward conversation, the person who annoys you, the thing you haven’t finished. “Ah!” says the voice, “a miserable day will this be.” And we drag ourselves through the day weighed down.

Meyer makes a key distinction:

“God is pledged to give strength for all duties which He sets, but not for the burdens which we elect to take on as well.”

God gives you strength for today’s tasks. But if you also carry tomorrow’s worries, next year’s fears and a hundred “what ifs”, you are carrying a load he never asked you to pick up.

Meyer’s cure is simple: hand them over. “Treat the burden of care as once the burden of sin; kneel down and deliberately hand it over to Jesus.” He suggests praying something like: “Lord, I entrust to thee this, and this, and this. I can not carry them.”

He quotes the poet George Herbert, who said we must put our worries “all into Christ’s bag.” And he asks: if you have ever handed a problem to a strong, trustworthy friend and felt the relief, can’t Jesus, who loved you enough to die for you, be trusted with the smaller things of your daily life?

Meyer also says that our worried faces send a message to the people around us. He says we are either “libels or Bibles”: either we give a false picture of God, as if he can’t be trusted, or we show what he is really like.

Handing worries to God doesn’t mean pretending everything is fine, or never planning. And if anxiety is overwhelming, if you can’t sleep, can’t stop worrying, or have panic attacks, please talk to a trusted adult or a doctor as well. God often helps us through other people.

One thing to do this week: tonight, write down every worry on your mind. Then pray through the list, handing each one to Jesus: “Lord, I give you this.” Put the list away. Each time a worry comes back this week, say: “That’s in Christ’s bag.”

study_questions.question: What voice does Meyer describe in the morning?
study_questions.answer: A voice listing everything that will go wrong and telling us it will be a miserable day.

study_questions.question: What does God promise strength for, and what not?
study_questions.answer: Strength for the duties he sets, but not for the extra burdens we choose to take on.

study_questions.question: What does Meyer mean by “libels or Bibles”?
study_questions.answer: Our lives either give a false picture of God or show what he is really like, depending partly on how we carry our burdens.

fields.title: When Life Hurts
fields.body_html:
“God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.” — Psalm 46:1 (KJV)

Meyer’s chapter on sorrow is written for people going through something really painful: a friendship or relationship that has ended, a family breaking up, illness, moving away, or someone they love dying.

First, he reminds us that we are not alone. Countless people have walked this road before us, including Jesus himself. He says Jesus “trod this difficult path, leaving traces of His blood on its flints.”

Second, he says something very important:

“Do not talk about punishment.”

When something bad happens, it is easy to think, “God must be punishing me.” Meyer says no. All the punishment for our sins was laid on Jesus. If God were still punishing us, it would mean Jesus’ suffering wasn’t enough.

Meyer believed God can use hard times like a refiner uses fire to purify silver. He pictures God sitting by the furnace, watching carefully, controlling the heat, never letting it go further than we can bear, and waiting to see his own face reflected in the silver.

But one thing needs saying clearly. Not everything that happens to us is God’s plan. If someone is hurting you, through abuse, bullying, or cruelty, that is never God’s will for you, and it is not something you should simply accept. Please tell a trusted adult.

Meyer’s most comforting advice is to keep reminding yourself that Jesus is with you, even when you don’t feel it: “Dare to repeat it often, though you do not feel it … ‘Thou art with me.’”

He says that friends often try to cheer us up with things like “time heals” or suggestions to keep busy, and sometimes that leaves us feeling more alone. But Jesus is closer than they are, “knowing each throb of pain”, waiting to comfort us like a mother comforting a tired, hurting child.

And one day, Meyer says, the comfort you receive will become something you can give to others who are hurting.

If you are grieving, it is good to talk about it. A parent, a youth leader, a school counsellor or a grief support service can help you through.

One thing to do this week: if you are going through something painful, say Psalm 23:4 to yourself several times a day this week: “Thou art with me.” And tell one trusted person how you are really feeling.

study_questions.question: Why does Meyer say not to talk about punishment?
study_questions.answer: Because all the punishment for our sins was laid on Jesus; God is not punishing his children.

study_questions.question: What picture does Meyer use for how God can use suffering?
study_questions.answer: A refiner sitting by the furnace, controlling the heat and waiting to see his face reflected in the silver.

study_questions.question: What does Meyer say to repeat even when you don’t feel it?
study_questions.answer: “Thou art with me.”

fields.title: Christ in You
fields.body_html:
“To whom God would make known what is the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles; which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.” — Colossians 1:27 (KJV)

Meyer’s last chapters go to the heart of everything: Jesus doesn’t just guide us from the outside. He lives in us by his Spirit.

Paul called this a mystery: “Christ in you, the hope of glory.” Meyer imagines asking Jesus, “Master, where dwellest thou?”, as the first disciples did. Today, he says, Jesus would not point to heaven or to a grand church building, “but to the happy spirit that loves, trusts, and obeys Him.”

Jesus said: “Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him.” Meyer says Jesus wants to live in each believer “as a tenant in a house; as sap in the branch”.

Meyer also writes about the presence of God. God is always near, he says, but we don’t always realise it. He mentions Brother Lawrence, the monastery cook, who for years lived with a constant sense of God’s presence while doing ordinary jobs.

And he writes about being filled with the Holy Spirit. He says many Christians have the Spirit only “as an attenuated thread, a silver streak, a shallow brook”, when God wants to fill them like a full river. Do you lack assurance? Victory over sin? Power to serve? Meyer says the answer is the Holy Spirit. Paul’s command is simple: “Be filled with the Spirit.”

This is the real secret of guidance. It isn’t a technique. It is a relationship. When Jesus lives in you, and you keep saying yes to him, he guides you from the inside.

Meyer lived to be eighty-one. A few days before he died in 1929, he wrote to a friend:

“It may be that before this reaches you, I shall have entered the palace. Don’t trouble to write. We shall meet in the morning.”

He had followed God’s guidance all his life, one step at a time, and he finished with complete confidence. The God who guided him promises to guide you too, not the whole way at once, but the next step, and the next, all the way home.

One thing to do this week: read Revelation 3:20 this week. Each morning, pray: “Lord Jesus, you live in me. Fill me with your Spirit today, and guide my next step.” Notice one moment each day when you sense him leading.

study_questions.question: Where does Meyer say Jesus would point today if asked where he lives?
study_questions.answer: Not to heaven or a grand building but to the happy spirit that loves, trusts and obeys him.

study_questions.question: How does Meyer describe Christians who have the Spirit only a little?
study_questions.answer: As having him like an attenuated thread, a silver streak or a shallow brook, rather than a full river.

study_questions.question: What did Meyer write to a friend just before he died?
study_questions.answer: “It may be that before this reaches you, I shall have entered the palace. Don’t trouble to write. We shall meet in the morning.”
